conclusion.label: hedged

report:
## Does Hypnosis Help with Smoking Cessation?

**Conclusion: The premise is only partly correct.** The most rigorous evidence—the Cochrane systematic review—does not conclude hypnosis doesn't work; rather, it concludes the evidence is too weak and inconsistent to determine whether hypnotherapy is effective for smoking cessation, one way or the other. This is an important distinction from a definitive "no."

**What the evidence shows:**

The Cochrane Review on hypnotherapy for smoking cessation (updated through 2019) is the gold-standard synthesis of randomized controlled trials in this area. According to summaries of that review, "the evidence is insufficient to determine if hypnotherapy is more effective than other treatments" (https://hypnosiscredentials.com/hypnosis/research/hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/). A related Cochrane umbrella review (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2021) similarly "concluded uncertainty about the effects of hypnosis" when compared across smoking cessation interventions (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full).

This uncertainty stems from methodological weaknesses in the underlying trials—small sample sizes, inconsistent hypnosis protocols, and high risk of bias—rather than from clear evidence of no effect.

More recent, broader research paints a more optimistic but less rigorous picture. A 2025 systematic review by Ekanayake & Elkins, which examined 63 studies (a much larger pool than Cochrane's stricter RCT-only inclusion criteria), found that "66.7% of well-designed studies reported a positive impact of hypnosis for smoking cessation" (https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/). However, this review used a "wider-lens approach" than Cochrane, likely including lower-quality or non-randomized studies, which may inflate apparent effectiveness.

**Bottom line:** Rather than "no," the accurate scientific answer is "unproven"—the highest-quality evidence (Cochrane) shows insufficient certainty to confirm hypnosis works better than no treatment or other interventions, while lower-rigor reviews suggest more promise. Conventional treatments (counseling, medication) remain better supported.
